paragraphs.text:
Scientific research and technological innovation support one another and can profoundly change methods of investigation and production.
Astronomy is an ancient science, and space technology makes it possible to observe the universe from beyond Earth's atmosphere.

Molecular biology and genetics have advanced the study of life processes, while progress in chemistry has expanded the chemical industry's ability to synthesize and produce substances.
Geology, meteorology, oceanography and other natural sciences also develop through new theories, instruments and methods.

Technologies for energy, materials, production and infrastructure continue to develop.
Changes in electricity generation include using nuclear energy alongside the combustion of fossil fuels, rather than an inevitable conversion of every fossil-fuel power station to a nuclear plant.

Materials science enables the manufacture of materials with particular useful properties, and mechanization and automation have changed many industrial and agricultural processes.
Technological improvements also provide ways to improve the efficiency and performance of transport, construction and communication.

Scientific development has increased science's influence on social life and production.
Through inventions, engineering design and practical application, scientific knowledge can become a productive capability.
Scientific achievements can improve the production of material goods that people need, but their practical effects also depend on organization, resources and the conditions of use.

Scientific and technological progress can support large-scale improvements in production.
Turning knowledge into reliable equipment, processes and infrastructure can help meet society's material needs.

The social effects of these improvements depend on how people organize and use technology;
they are not automatically guaranteed by a political system or by technological development itself.

Physics is an important foundation of modern natural science.
The laws it investigates and the instruments it develops influence many fields of research, technology and production.
Examples from astronomy, the life sciences, energy and electronics illustrate these connections.

For thousands of years, astronomical observations relied mainly on visible light, which occupies only a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Advances in radio physics made radio astronomy another means of observation and broadened our understanding of the universe.

Observations in different radio bands complement visible-light observations and help investigate celestial objects that were previously difficult to detect or understand.
Neutrinos provide a carrier of astronomical information in addition to electromagnetic radiation.

Neutrinos can carry information from stellar interiors, and observations of solar neutrinos help investigate nuclear reactions in the Sun's core.
Their interpretation must also account for neutrinos changing type as they travel.

Nuclear and particle physics provide the theoretical and experimental foundations for neutrino detection.
Neutrino astronomy has not settled whether macroscopic worlds made of antiparticles exist, and the universe's matter-antimatter asymmetry remains a subject of research.

Earth's atmosphere absorbs electromagnetic radiation from many parts of the spectrum, so ground-based observations use particular bands that can pass through it.
Sending instruments beyond the atmosphere provides information that is difficult to receive at the surface.

Space observations extend ultraviolet, infrared, $x$ ray and $\gamma$ ray astronomy and allow the study of primary cosmic rays before they interact with the atmosphere.
Different instruments detect different bands and particles.

This does not mean that every kind of particle and radiation can already be observed.
These observations have greatly expanded astronomy's sources of information, with an important contribution from detection methods and recording instruments developed in physics.
Combining astronomy with physics allows astrophysics to investigate the properties and processes of celestial objects more deeply.

Molecular biology and genetics investigate the molecular basis of life processes and the transmission and action of genetic information.
Molecules are material components of living systems, not tiny organisms that live independently.

Researchers use electron microscopy and charged-particle-beam methods, $x$ ray structural analysis, electron imaging, neutron analysis, isotope tracing and ultracentrifugation to observe, separate or investigate biological samples.
These methods have different domains of use and are not all the same kind of microscopic imaging.

They use physical principles such as interactions of particles or radiation with matter, radioactivity and rotational motion.
Theories, instruments and experimental methods from physics work together with biological and chemical research to deepen our understanding of life processes.

Theories and experimental methods from physics also help chemistry, geology, oceanography and other natural sciences investigate the properties of matter and natural processes.
Their development illustrates how different sciences support one another.

Physics also provides a scientific foundation for many technological developments.
Energy engineering, communication, transport, construction and industrial and agricultural production can use physical laws and research findings to improve equipment and processes.
Such improvements also require contributions from other disciplines and engineering practice.

Nuclear energy gives energy engineering a pathway distinct from burning chemical fuels.
For equal masses, complete fission of fissile material can release several million times as much energy as burning coal;

this is not a ratio of the actual electricity output or efficiency of two power stations.
The potential energy of nuclear-fuel resources depends on usable materials, fuel cycles and technological conditions.

Underground reserves alone do not establish that practically available nuclear energy must exceed the energy available from fossil fuels.
Coal, oil and natural gas serve both as fuels and as raw materials for the chemical industry, and burning large quantities consumes these finite resources.

Uranium can be used as nuclear fuel, and thorium also has potential in suitable nuclear fuel cycles, but their use is not free of resource or environmental costs.
High energy density is an important characteristic of nuclear energy.
Its practical use must also consider safety, radioactive waste and resource management.

Controlled nuclear fusion has the potential to supply energy, but it cannot guarantee that humanity will never face energy problems again.
Turning fusion reactions into reliable electricity generation requires solutions for sustaining the reaction, using its energy, materials and engineering.

Nuclear physics provides a scientific foundation for both fission and fusion energy.
Practical power systems also need support from other fields of physics and engineering.

**Modern technology can use materials whose properties are designed for particular purposes**, but these materials still require material feedstocks and do not eliminate the use of natural resources.
Material synthesis and processing allow properties to be adjusted to technological needs.

Physical methods using electron beams, ion beams, laser beams, strong magnetic fields, high pressure, high temperature and ultrasound can be combined with chemical methods to prepare or treat suitable materials.
They can produce particular material properties and new ways of processing materials, thereby improving production processes.

Many production processes in industry and agriculture can be automated.
Automated systems measure the state of a process and use electronic controls to adjust equipment operation.

Measuring, monitoring and control instruments provide the information and means needed for this operation.
Their design draws on radio electronics, solid-state physics and other fields of physics, while some measurement methods also use results from nuclear physics.

Physics provides an important foundation for electronic computing.
Early electronic computers are commonly grouped into three generations according to their main devices: vacuum tubes, transistors and integrated circuits①.

This historical classification does not mean that computer development ended there.
Physical research on devices and materials helps reduce circuit size and improve computational speed and reliability.

Laser technology and holographic techniques, which use coherent light to record and reconstruct optical information, also provide approaches for research in optical information processing and related computing technologies.
This does not establish that they will generally replace electronic circuits.

① An integrated circuit forms many electronic components and their connections on a small chip, instead of linking a collection of separate components one by one with external wires.
Manufacturing can change local semiconductor properties by introducing impurity atoms and can also form and pattern thin films on the surface.

These steps produce devices with particular structures and electrical functions.
They cannot simply be described as layers of a particular kind of molecule.
Miniaturization can put part of a radio's circuitry on a chip the size of a match head, but the chip is not a complete radio with its antenna, power supply and other components.

These examples do not cover every influence of physics on science and technology, but they show its close connections with many fields. **Modern physics has made important contributions to scientific and technological development**, working together with other disciplines and engineering practice.

Understanding the basic laws of nature, especially through physics, helps people understand technology and continue developing science and engineering.
Applying this knowledge to practical problems provides means to improve production and meet human needs.
Technological capability by itself does not determine how society distributes goods or guarantee the realization of a particular social ideal.
